claude_take: Today's stories keep circling the same question: who gets paid for value someone else created, and who gets to decide. Believe's about-face on Suno and AMC's nine-year Walking Dead settlement both show institutions eventually choosing to pay rather than keep fighting, while the NSA's distillation advisory says China's AI labs are choosing to just take it instead -- and TIFF building its own market and Shaun Leane finally stepping into his own name are, in their own ways, about that same instinct to own what you make rather than let someone else profit from it. That strain shows up more starkly when the referees themselves stop agreeing: two courts can't settle which map governs Missouri's election, and Americans' trust in the public school system just hit a record low. None of this is really about AI or politics specifically -- it's about how much weight our institutions are being asked to carry right now, and how visibly some of them are buckling.
claude_take_title: Who Gets Paid, Who Decides, and Who Just Takes It

items.headline: NSA, FBI and CISA Accuse Six Chinese AI Firms of Industrial-Scale Model Distillation
items.summary: The three agencies issued a joint advisory naming DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot AI, MiniMax, StepFun and Z.AI, accusing them of systematically extracting the capabilities of US frontier models -- including Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's GPT and Google's Gemini -- through industrial-scale knowledge distillation since late 2024. The advisory says the firms used fraudulent accounts, bulk subscriptions and proxy "transfer stations" to pull billions of tokens across millions of queries, and recommends US AI companies quietly degrade responses to suspected distillation accounts rather than banning them outright. It adds a rare joint intelligence-community voice to a long-running dispute over how much of China's AI progress rests on copying, rather than independently developing, American models.

items.headline: Suno Strikes Global Licensing Deal With Believe and TuneCore, Ending Months of Blocking
items.summary: Believe and its self-release platform TuneCore have signed a strategic partnership with AI music generator Suno, just over four months after Believe began blocking Suno-made tracks from its distribution pipeline. Under the deal, Believe and TuneCore artists and labels can opt in to license their catalogs into Suno's new industry-partner models, and tracks made with those models become eligible for distribution through Believe and TuneCore. It's the first such agreement Suno has struck with an independent distributor, following earlier licensing deals with Warner Music and BMG, and marks a shift from confrontation toward a negotiated, opt-in model for compensating rights holders.

items.headline: AMC Settles Nine-Year 'Walking Dead' Profit-Participation Lawsuit for $120 Million
items.summary: AMC Networks has agreed to pay $120 million to five "Walking Dead" producers -- including creator Robert Kirkman, Gale Anne Hurd, David Alpert, Charles Eglee and Glen Mazzara -- to settle a lawsuit over how the network calculated the profits it owed them, avoiding a federal trial that was set to begin in October. AMC will pay $85 million this month and $35 million by January 2027, with the second payment also counting as an advance against the producers' future profit participation, so they keep sharing in the franchise's earnings going forward. The case turned on AMC's formula for "modified adjusted gross receipts," the same dispute that led the network to pay director Frank Darabont and CAA $200 million in a related 2021 settlement.

items.headline: Toronto Film Festival Launches Its First Official Content Market
items.summary: The Toronto International Film Festival opened a new official content market this week, backed by a C$23 million investment from the Canadian government, aimed at making Toronto a North American hub for buying and selling film, TV and immersive projects. Organizers are pitching it as a way to bridge the long gap in the festival-market calendar between Cannes and Berlin, giving the festival a more structured marketplace than its previous informal deal-making. The launch comes as Canada's film sector looks to capitalize on the current US political and trade climate to pull more production and dealmaking north.

items.headline: Dueling Court Rulings Leave Missouri's Congressional Map in Chaos
items.summary: Days after the Missouri Supreme Court unanimously blocked the legislature's Republican-drawn congressional map and ordered it to a November referendum, a federal judge ordered the state to use that same map anyway, ruling that switching maps this late would disenfranchise voters since the primary already happened in August. The order came within minutes of Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh declining to intervene in the state case, leaving two courts flatly contradicting each other over which map governs the November election. The map at issue targets the Kansas City-area seat held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver II, part of a broader wave of mid-decade partisan gerrymandering ahead of the midterms.

items.headline: Americans' Satisfaction With K-12 Education Hits a Record Low
items.summary: Just 32% of US adults say they're satisfied with the quality of the country's K-12 education, according to a new Gallup/Walton Family Foundation poll -- the lowest mark since Gallup began asking the question 27 years ago, and an 11-point drop over just two years. The decline spans party lines and reflects both a widening political divide over what schools should teach and growing doubts that schools are preparing students for college and future jobs. Notably, the poll found a disconnect with how students themselves feel: Gen Z students actually rated their own schools somewhat more positively than in recent years.

items.headline: Alexander McQueen's Longtime Jeweller Shaun Leane Launches His Own House
items.summary: Shaun Leane, the jewellery designer behind some of Alexander McQueen's most extreme 1990s runway pieces, is launching an independent label called 12, focused on bespoke high jewellery and sculptural objects. The move lets Leane build a namesake business around the same boundary-pushing, sculptural approach he brought to McQueen's shows for decades, rather than working under someone else's house. It's part of a broader pattern this year of veteran creative talents stepping out from behind established maisons to build labels under their own names.

items.headline: Mill's Harm Principle
items.headline_fr: Le principe de non-nuisance de John Stuart Mill
items.summary: In "On Liberty" (1859), John Stuart Mill argued that the only legitimate reason society can exercise power over an individual against their will is to prevent harm to others -- not to make them happier, wiser, or more virtuous by someone else's lights. This "harm principle" became the foundational argument for why the state should stay out of decisions that affect mainly the person making them, even unwise or unpopular ones. It remains the default reference point in debates over free speech, drug policy, and personal autonomy -- and its limits show up whenever "harm" gets stretched to cover offense, self-harm, or diffuse harm to society rather than a concrete injury to a specific other person.
items.summary_fr: Dans De la liberté (1859), John Stuart Mill soutient que la seule raison légitime pour la société d'exercer un pouvoir sur un individu contre sa volonté est d'empêcher qu'il ne nuise à autrui -- et non de le rendre plus heureux, plus sage ou plus vertueux selon les critères de quelqu'un d'autre. Ce "principe de non-nuisance" est devenu l'argument fondateur expliquant pourquoi l'État doit s'abstenir d'intervenir dans les décisions qui concernent avant tout la personne qui les prend, même si elles paraissent imprudentes ou impopulaires. Il reste la référence incontournable dans les débats sur la liberté d'expression, les politiques en matière de drogues et l'autonomie personnelle -- et ses limites apparaissent chaque fois que la notion de "nuisance" s'étend au simple malaise, à l'atteinte à soi-même ou à un tort diffus envers la société plutôt qu'à un préjudice concret causé à autrui.
